questions.q: A person purchases a laptop for their freelance graphic design work from home. Under the Consumer Protection Act, how is this buyer classified, and why?
questions.a: The buyer is an **Individual Consumer** (self-employment category). The Act explicitly includes goods bought for "self-employment" to earn a livelihood as consumer purchases. A wrong answer (e.g., "commercial buyer" or "reseller") reveals the misconception that any income-generating use makes the purchase commercial — the law distinguishes self-employment (livelihood) from resale (profit from trading).

questions.q: Explain in your own words why a hospital buying MRI machines is classified differently from a medical equipment distributor buying the same machines, even though both are organisations.
questions.a: The hospital is an **Institutional Consumer** because it uses the MRI machines to provide healthcare services (end-use). The distributor is a **Reseller** because it buys to sell further for profit. A wrong answer that labels both as "institutional buyers" or both as "consumers" shows the student is classifying by *buyer type* (organisation) rather than *purpose of purchase* (end-use vs. resale) — the core distinction in consumer law.

questions.q: A farmer buys a tractor for ploughing his own fields. A contractor buys an identical tractor to rent out to farmers. Classify both buyers and justify using the "purpose test".
questions.a: Farmer → **Individual Consumer** (self-employment in agriculture). Contractor → **Reseller/Intermediary** (providing rental service is a commercial activity; the tractor is a capital asset for business income). Steps: (1) Identify buyer's primary activity; (2) Determine if goods are for end-use or for providing service for profit; (3) Apply purpose test. A wrong answer classifying the contractor as a consumer misses that *renting out* is a commercial service — the tractor is not for the contractor's own consumption.

questions.q: Compare the consumer status of: (a) a government school buying mid-day meal ingredients, (b) a government corporation buying steel to build a bridge. Are both "Government Consumers"? Why or why not?
questions.a: (a) **Government Consumer** — ingredients are consumed in service delivery (feeding children). (b) **Not a consumer** — steel is an input for infrastructure creation (capital formation), not for direct consumption in service provision. The distinction lies in whether the purchase is for *direct service delivery* (consumer) or *asset creation/production* (non-consumer). A wrong answer labelling both as government consumers fails to apply the "end-use in service" criterion.

questions.q: Critique this statement: "Any buyer who pays money for a product is a consumer and deserves protection under the Consumer Protection Act." Use the classification framework to defend your position.
questions.a: The statement is **false**. The Act protects only those purchasing for *personal, household, or self-employment use* — excluding resellers, commercial enterprises buying inputs for production, and buyers for capital asset creation. Example: A factory buying raw cotton to make cloth is a commercial buyer, not a consumer. The error is conflating "buyer" (transaction role) with "consumer" (legal status based on purpose). Protection is purpose-specific, not transaction-universal.

questions.q: Design a 3-question checklist that a consumer forum lawyer would use to determine if a new client qualifies as a "consumer" under the Act. Each question must test a different classification boundary.
questions.a: Good checklist: (1) "Was the good/service bought for your own use, your family's use, or to earn your livelihood through self-employment?" — tests Individual vs. Reseller boundary. (2) "Are you purchasing on behalf of an organisation — and if so, will the item be used directly in delivering the organisation's services (e.g., hospital buying medicines) or as input for production/resale?" — tests Institutional vs. Commercial boundary. (3) "Is the purchase funded by government and meant for direct public service delivery (e.g., school textbooks) or for infrastructure/production (e.g., cement for a dam)?" — tests Government Consumer vs. Non-consumer boundary. A poor checklist asks only "Did you pay?" or "Are you a person?" — missing purpose entirely.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: A consumer is any person who buys goods or avails services for personal use, household consumption, or self-employment purposes, in exchange for ______ (money, promise of payment, or deferred payment).

Fill in the blank: Imagine you walk into a supermarket and see three shoppers: a mother buying milk for her child, a school principal ______ 500 notebooks for students, and a kirana store owner buying the same notebooks to sell in his shop.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can correctly classify a given buyer scenario into one of the four consumer categories, justify the classification using the "purpose of purchase" criterion, and explain why resellers are excluded from the legal definition of "consumer" under the Consumer Protection Act.
